messages.subject: Strange predicted values
parts:
Hi,

I'm just starting to use stan for some basic regression tasks.  After several days of running, I have my first 100 samples from the posterior distribution for all betas.

This is a normal model:  y ~ normal(mu,sigma)
The true values of y range from about 15 to 20
All covariates are centered at 0 and have unit variance.

As part of getting comfortable with stan, I wanted to manually calculate the predicted values and compare the distribution to the true values to see how things looked.  So, I just took the first case of my data and multiplied it by the posterior samples from the betas.  The values I ranged from -439 to 2168.   Clearly not correct.  I tested this with several other cases and also saw a huge range of values, none of which were even close to even the true range of y.

Am I misunderstanding something here?  Is this the correct procedure to utilize the betas?

Thank You

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange predicted values
parts:
It would be easier to help you if you sent us
the code for the model you ran. (And either send
us the data or let us know its size at least.)

You can look at the R-hat values to see if you've
converged.

You can also try initializing all coefficients to 0;
there's an option from both the command line and from
RStan. Regressions with very many predictors can be
very unstable when initialized with Stan's highly
dispersed values. If you want to get fancy, initialize
the coeffs to 0 and mu to the mean of the y in the data.
Alternatively, standardize the y (this affects prior
specifications, but shouldn't matter if you have pretty broad
priors).

If you have the fit, you should be able to check it
against your existing data by calculating the model predictions
and looking at their errors versus the observed data.
You'd usually want to do this for all samples and take
the average to do full Bayesian posterior inference.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Strange predicted values
parts:
On Wednesday, January 2, 2013 10:34:09 PM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
I'm just starting to use stan for some basic regression tasks.  After several days of running, I have my first 100 samples from the posterior distribution for all betas.
Something is seriously wrong. For a model like this, 100 samples should be instantaneous.

This is a normal model:  y ~ normal(mu,sigma)
The true values of y range from about 15 to 20
All covariates are centered at 0 and have unit variance.

I suspect you are falling victim to inappropriate missing values. If the coefficients (including the intercept) are roughly zero to start with, and the mean of y is roughly 17.5, then it is starting in an area of essentially zero posterior mass. To rectify this, you can either center y or do something like this in your .stan file:

data {
  ...
}
transformed data {
  real mean_y;
  mean_y <- mean(y);
}
parameters {
  real intercept_shift;
  real betas[K-1];
}
transformed parameters {
  real intercept;
  intercept <- mean_y + intercept_shift;
}
model {
  ...
}


That way, even if intercept_shift is roughly zero, the intercept is roughly appropriate for y.

Ben

On Thursday, January 3, 2013 12:58:40 AM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
The actual data is about 40000 cases of 200 covariates.

Now I see how it could take a while. It would be much faster if you use matrix algebra. Something like:

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  real y[N];
  matrix[N,K] X; // possibly including a column of ones
}
parameters {
  real betas[K];
  real<lower=0,upper=1> sigma_betas;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> sigma_y;
}
model {
  betas ~ normal(0,sigma_betas);
  y ~ normal(X * betas, sigma_y);
}

The above presumes that y has been centered as I suggested in my other post. Your code implicitly has an intercept of 1.0, which is still a long way off if the mean of the outcome is 17.5.

Ben

+ b_var_1 * var_1[i]

then yes, that could kill the performance. The reason is that it has to do roughly 200 * N auto-diffs per evaluation of the log-posterior. Markus optimized the differentiation of the X * beta construction, so it is much better if you can write the model with as much matrix algebra as possible.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange predicted values
parts: On Thursday, January 3, 2013 2:10:22 AM UTC-5, Noah wrote:
Ben,

That makes sense.  Currently I am doing it the *slow* way.

My understanding was that each covariate was a vector in stan.  How can I combine them all into a single matrix so that I may then use matrix algebra?  Is there an example online somewhere that I can study?

Each covariate *can* be a vector but need not be. And as you discovered, doing so can lead to computational problems.

The easiest thing to do is to write the matrix to a file as a matrix and then read it as a matrix in the data {} block. There are examples of this in the manual. If you are using RStan, there is a function called stan_rdump() that facilitates this. Just make a data.frame of covariates called X (in addition to a y vector) and do something like:

stan_rdump(c("y", X"), file = "my_data.R")

If you are not using R, then let us know and we can probably provide suggestions.

If all else fails, you could read the data in as vectors and use a transformed data {} block to glue them together into a matrix, roughly:

data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;

...
}
transformed data {
  real mean_y;

matrix[N,K] X;
  mean_y <- mean(y);
  for(i in 1:N) {
    X[i,1] <- x_var_1[i];
    X[i,2] <- x_var_2[i];
    ...
    X[i,200] <- x_var_200[i];
  }
}
parameters {
  real intercept_shift;
  vector[K] betas;

real<lower=0,upper=1> sigma_betas;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> sigma_y;
}
model {
  betas ~ normal(0,sigma_betas);

y ~ normal(mean_y + intercept_shift + X * beta, sigma_y);
}

Ben
